title: Randomized Controlled Trials of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: Systematic Review
authors: Thomas Y. T. Lam et al.

reading.body:
Only 39 of 11,839 retrieved articles were randomised trials of AI in clinical practice, so the clinical evidence base is far thinner than the volume of published work suggests.

The ratio is the finding. A search of five databases through July 2021 returned 11,839 records, and 0.33 percent of them met the standard of a randomised comparison against care without AI. The trials that exist are concentrated rather than broad: 13 specialties, with gastroenterology and endoscopy accounting for 15 of the 39. They are also geographically narrow, split roughly evenly across North America, Europe, and Asia.

Where trials have been run, the results lean positive. AI-supported care outperformed standard care in 30 of 39 trials, and 21 of those 30 improved outcomes that matter clinically. That is a promising signal, but it rests on small samples and single-centre designs, which limit how far the results generalise to other hospitals, populations, and workflows.

This data covers published randomised evidence up to July 2021 and nothing about deployment, cost, or compute. It cannot say how much AI is actually running in clinics, what hardware or power it requires, or whether the positive trial results hold at scale. The gap it measures is a gap in evidence, not in adoption.

explain_beginner: This review examined medical studies where artificial intelligence helped with patient care. Researchers searched five databases up to July 2021 and found 11,839 articles, but only 39 were randomized trials that compared AI supported care with standard care. These trials came from North America, Europe, and Asia and covered 13 specialties, often gastroenterology and endoscopy. In 30 of 39 trials, AI supported care did better than standard care. In 21 of those 30, the improvement was meaningful for patients. The main message is that AI in medicine shows promise, but the evidence base is still small and needs more trials.
explain_business: For executives, this review suggests AI in clinical care has promising but limited proof. Researchers found only 39 randomized trials among 11,839 articles, so the evidence base is thin. The trials covered 13 specialties, often gastroenterology and endoscopy, and came from North America, Europe, and Asia. In 30 of 39 trials, AI supported care beat standard care, and 21 of those 30 improved outcomes that matter clinically. However, small samples and single center designs reduce confidence and generalizability. A practical decision is to adopt cautiously, ask for larger multi center trials, and treat current AI adoption claims as early evidence rather than settled proof.
explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and searched CINAHL, Cochrane Central, Embase, MEDLINE, and PubMed through July 2021 for randomized trials comparing AI supported tools with standard care without AI. From 11,839 records, 39 trials, 0.33%, met inclusion. Trials were roughly evenly split across North America, Europe, and Asia, spanned 13 specialties, and concentrated in gastroenterology, with 15 endoscopy studies. Most used biosignal based AI, fewer used clinical data. AI supported interventions outperformed standard care in 30 of 39 trials, and 21 of those 30 showed improvement in outcomes that matter clinically. Small samples and single center designs limited generalizability.
